contexts.title: What the bill ends
contexts.html:
This bill would end the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending the emergency would cancel the tariffs based on it: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries. The bill would not end tariffs under other laws.

If enacted, S.J.Res.88 ends the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, in Executive Order 14257, on the date of enactment.

The bill says “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [SES 1]

When this emergency ends, the extra import taxes imposed because of it stop for new imports at the rates in force that day. Other tariff laws are not ended, and matters already pending or duties already owed are not changed by the ending itself.

Later orders changed the rates, but the emergency stayed their basis: “the terms of Executive Order 14257, as amended, shall continue to apply.” [UNN 2]

Federal law says that when an emergency ends, “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [SES 2]. The Center for American Progress, a policy group that favors ending these taxes, says that ending this emergency “would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [UNN 3]

contexts.title: How Congress can end an emergency
contexts.html:
The National Emergencies Act lets Congress end a national emergency by enacting a joint resolution, and this bill uses that method.

The President declares a national emergency. The law also gives Congress a way to end one. The Congressional Research Service explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [UNC 24]

An emergency ends if “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” [SES 2]. The bill says it acts “pursuant to section 202 of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622)” [SES 1].

contexts.title: The order’s power to raise these taxes
contexts.html:
The April 2 order let the President raise these taxes further, including if another country retaliated or if U.S. manufacturing worsened. Ending the emergency ends that power under this order, but not tariff powers under other laws.

The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [SES 23] It also says: “Should U.S. manufacturing capacity and output continue to worsen, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase duties under this order.” [UNC 10]

contexts.title: The October 2025 trade deals
contexts.html:
The trade deals signed with Malaysia and Cambodia on October 26, 2025, and the framework with Thailand, set U.S. tax terms under this emergency alongside promises by those countries. They were not yet in force on October 30, 2025.

These deals are called Agreements on Reciprocal Trade.

In Malaysia's deal the United States will “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [UNC 26] and identify goods “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [UNC 26] The September order says relief depends on factors including “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [UNN 29]. Malaysia's enforcement article says: “If a Party considers that the other Party has not complied with a provision of this Agreement, the Party may review the terms of this Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [UNN 35] Cambodia's agreement has a similar article [UNN 36].

nodes.title: Less cost pressure on households
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would reduce cost pressure on households buying covered imported goods, even if some prices would not fall fully or quickly.

nodes.title: Less uncertain future tariff rates
nodes.claim_html: Ending this emergency would make future U.S. tariff rates at least somewhat less uncertain and less subject to sudden change, even though other tariff powers would remain.

nodes.title: One source of trade conflict removed
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes, and the order’s power to raise them if another country retaliates, would remove one source of trade conflict between the United States and other countries.

nodes.title: China more likely to lower its retaliatory charge
nodes.claim_html: Ending the U.S. emergency taxes would make China more likely to lower the retaliatory charge it added on U.S. goods in response to them.

nodes.title: Less leverage for carrying out the signed deals
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would remove an incentive and an enforcement tool for getting Malaysia and Cambodia to carry out the promises in their signed deals, including promises on market access, labor rights, the environment, security and supply, public rule-making and internet rules.

nodes.title: Less pressure on Thailand and Cambodia to keep the peace
nodes.claim_html: Ending this emergency would remove a tariff incentive the President had used to press Thailand and Cambodia toward a ceasefire, weakening pressure on both to keep the peace and keep talking.

nodes.title: Less price protection for U.S. factory work
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would remove some price protection for U.S. makers of competing goods, putting some U.S. factory work and pay at risk, including jobs open to people with limited job options.

nodes.title: Weaker support for U.S. backup production of medical gloves
nodes.claim_html: Ending the tax would remove a price advantage for U.S.-made medical gloves and weaken support for keeping U.S. production available when overseas supplies are disrupted.

nodes.title: A smaller incentive to make military batteries in the U.S.
nodes.claim_html: Ending the tax on imported battery packs would remove an extra incentive to buy U.S.-made batteries and invest in their production, including batteries the military needs.

nodes.title: Less friction with defense partners
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would remove a source of distrust and political resistance to defense and economic cooperation with partners such as Australia and New Zealand.

nodes.title: No emergency tariff pressure on EU environmental rules
nodes.claim_html: Ending the emergency would take away its import taxes as pressure on the European Union to weaken rules on companies’ climate and supply-chain duties.

nodes.title: No emergency tariff pressure for more shipped gas
nodes.claim_html: Ending the emergency would remove its tariff pressure on the European Union to buy more U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG), whose production and shipping add climate pollution compared with pipeline gas.

nodes.title: More demand for goods made by workers in poor countries
nodes.claim_html: Removing the added tax on goods from poor countries would support demand for those workers’ goods and investment in future production there.

nodes.title: Cheaper clean-power equipment
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported solar, battery and grid equipment would make it cheaper to install clean power and build clean-energy factories.

nodes.title: Easier making of pollution cleanup tools
nodes.claim_html: Ending the emergency would lower the cost of imported parts, or the time spent managing changing rates, for makers of tools that clean contaminated water.

nodes.title: Less cost pressure on water systems
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported water equipment would ease cost pressure on U.S. water utilities and reduce one cause of delayed maintenance, treatment and reuse projects.

nodes.title: Cheaper recycling machinery
nodes.claim_html: Ending the tax on covered imported recycling machinery would lower a cost of expanding recycling.

nodes.title: More orders for new clothing
nodes.claim_html: Lower prices for imported clothing would remove a restraint on orders and purchases of new clothing.

nodes.title: Money freed for small firms to operate and hire
nodes.claim_html: Lower import costs would free money that affected small firms need to operate and hire, and remove a burden they are less able to absorb than larger rivals.

nodes.title: Less cost and supply risk for hospital devices
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would reduce cost and supply risk for covered imported medical devices that U.S. hospitals use for surgery and infection control.

nodes.title: Lower charges to patients
nodes.claim_html: Lower hospital supply costs would ease pressure on patients’ medical bills and insurance charges.

nodes.title: Less pressure to cut hospital and ambulance staff or equipment
nodes.claim_html: Lower supply costs would ease pressure on hospitals and ambulance services to cut staff, services or spending on reliable equipment.

nodes.title: Lower costs for disease research
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported laboratory and device supplies would protect some research on better ways to prevent and treat disease.

nodes.title: Cheaper nutritious food
nodes.claim_html: Lower prices for covered imported fruit and other nutritious foods would lower a barrier to a healthy diet for some households.

nodes.title: More money left for medicine and care
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for everyday goods would leave some households more money for prescribed medicine and medical visits.

nodes.title: Less financial stress
nodes.claim_html: Ending this source of higher prices would remove a cause of financial worry for some people.

nodes.title: Cheaper alarms and fire alerts
nodes.claim_html: Ending the taxes on covered security and fire-safety products would lower a cost barrier to protecting homes.

nodes.title: Cheaper bicycle helmets
nodes.claim_html: Ending the taxes on covered imported helmets would lower a cost barrier to wearing protection while cycling.

nodes.title: Less pressure to cut workplace safety gear
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported safety equipment would ease pressure on employers to cut purchases of workplace protection.

nodes.title: Lower costs for military suppliers
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes on supplies outside the defense exemption would remove a cost from military suppliers and from what the military buys.

nodes.title: Cheaper supply options outside China
nodes.claim_html: Ending these taxes would lower the cost of importing covered goods from production sites outside China, making it easier to keep backup supply options.

nodes.title: Lower costs for cultural grocery stores
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for imported foods would help cultural grocery stores keep familiar foods on their shelves at prices their customers can afford.

nodes.title: Cheaper imported instruments for churches
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported musical instruments would reduce a cost for churches that buy or replace them.

nodes.title: Cheaper Christmas goods
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for covered imported Christmas trees and goods would cut a cost of buying or replacing what family Christmas customs use.

nodes.title: Cheaper imported religious teaching dolls
nodes.claim_html: Ending the remaining reciprocal tax would lower the cost of imported dolls sold as aids for teaching children Bible verses.

nodes.title: Less pressure on families’ church giving
nodes.claim_html: Lower household costs would ease pressure on some families’ ability to keep giving regular church offerings.

nodes.title: Cheaper toys for Christmas gift boxes
nodes.claim_html: Ending the tax on commercially imported toys would lower a cost of packing Christmas shoebox gifts for gospel outreach.

nodes.title: Less job insecurity harming workers’ health
nodes.claim_html: Lower import costs would reduce pressure on employers absorbing those costs to cut jobs, and the threat to workers’ health that job insecurity brings.

nodes.title: Less uncertainty holding back hiring and safety improvements
nodes.claim_html: Less uncertain tariff rates would remove a source of pressure on firms to hold back hiring, and on suppliers abroad to hold back workplace safety improvements.

nodes.title: Investment no longer held back by rate uncertainty
nodes.claim_html: Less uncertain tariff rates would help firms plan investments, including in production capacity the country needs.

nodes.title: Fewer tariff shocks to U.S. financial markets
nodes.claim_html: Ending this tariff program would remove a source of sudden policy news that has strained trading in U.S. government debt.

nodes.title: Less retaliation against U.S. export sales
nodes.claim_html: Fewer retaliatory taxes on U.S. exports would reduce a risk to export sales, including sales by farm families.

nodes.title: Less demand pressure on Brazilian forests and savannas
nodes.claim_html: Easing the U.S.–China tariff conflict would reduce one source of demand for Brazilian soy that threatens forests and savannas there.

nodes.title: Less resentment toward Asian Americans
nodes.claim_html: Removing one source of tariff conflict would reduce one source of resentment that leads some people to blame Asian Americans for another country’s actions.

nodes.title: Risk to marriage and family roles from lost factory pay
nodes.claim_html: Job and pay losses for men in factory work would reduce marriage and weaken husbands’ ability to provide for their families.

nodes.title: Risk to local congregations from lost factory work
nodes.claim_html: Lost local factory work would weaken some local congregations, as members lose income and younger people leave to find work.

nodes.title: Nature: cheaper clean power, cleanup, water reuse or recycling
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted helps protect nature: cheaper equipment for clean power that can replace fossil fuels, easier making of pollution cleanup tools, less cost pressure on water treatment and reuse projects that clean water and sustain habitats, or cheaper recycling machinery for cutting waste. Any one of them is a reason to favor the bill.

nodes.title: Nature: less pressure on Brazilian habitats
nodes.claim_html: Less demand pressure to clear Brazilian forests and savannas protects those habitats from destruction.

nodes.title: Nature: no tariff pressure against climate protection
nodes.claim_html: Whichever of these you accepted, removing tariff pressure to weaken EU climate and supply-chain rules, or to buy more U.S. shipped gas, defends nature against climate pollution and damage.

nodes.title: Nature: weaker pressure for environmental promises
nodes.claim_html: Malaysia and Cambodia promised action against illegal logging and wildlife trade, against overfishing, for careful use and recovery of materials, and for public input on rules. Weaker pressure to carry out any of these promises works against protecting nature, which gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Nature: more clothing production and waste
nodes.claim_html: More orders for new clothing create demand for production, materials, scarce water, transport and waste disposal, which harms nature and gives a reason to oppose losing the restraint.

nodes.title: Concern: easing costs where money is tightest
nodes.claim_html: Lower costs for necessities ease pressure on poorer households, which spend more of their income on goods and have little room to cut. Protecting those least able to pay serves concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting livelihoods
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted protects people’s chance to earn a living: money freed for small firms to operate and hire, less uncertainty holding back hiring and safety improvements, or less retaliation against export sales by farm families and others. Any one of them supports fair opportunities for workers and owners.

nodes.title: Concern: earnings for workers in poor countries
nodes.claim_html: More demand for their goods protects workers in poor countries, many of them women with few other ways to earn a living, and their families’ food, schooling and healthcare. That serves protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.

nodes.title: Concern: sparing small, poor economies a disproportionate burden
nodes.claim_html: Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people in small, poor economies that have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Burdens that reflect people’s circumstances and their part in a problem serve justice across borders.

nodes.title: Concern: review before burdens are imposed
nodes.claim_html: The emergency powers law lets the President set these taxes without the investigation other tariff laws usually require. Enforcing Congress’s check on that way of taxing supports public review of burdens placed on people’s food budgets and jobs, which serves just treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: vulnerable workers and their children
nodes.claim_html: Putting at risk factory work that opens doors to people with limited job options, including people with disabilities, endangers vulnerable workers and children who bear the costs of their parents’ lost work. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: weaker pressure for promises that protect vulnerable people
nodes.claim_html: The deals include promises on fair treatment of work from abroad, a Malaysian ban on imports made with forced labor, basic workplace protections, fishing safeguards for coastal families, and keeping a source of materials for medical tools open. Weaker pressure to carry out any of these promises works against protecting vulnerable people and fair treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: border communities and renewed fighting
nodes.claim_html: Less pressure to keep the peace raises the risk of renewed killing and displacement in border communities, which gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: food traditions and shared meeting places
nodes.claim_html: Helping cultural grocery stores keep familiar foods helps neighbors keep their own food traditions and keeps open places where people from different backgrounds meet and learn about each other’s cultures.

nodes.title: Tolerance: less blame of Asian Americans
nodes.claim_html: Less resentment that treats Asian Americans as enemies because of their ancestry supports tolerance toward all kinds of people.

nodes.title: Tolerance: weaker pressure for promises that protect people who differ
nodes.claim_html: The deals include promises against job discrimination, for migrant workers’ right to represent co-workers, for workers who organize and disagree with employers, for bans on goods made through the coercion of ethnic and religious minorities, for hearing people from other countries when making rules, and against an internet blocking rule. Weaker pressure to carry out any of these promises works against accepting and listening to people who are different.

nodes.title: Tolerance: dialogue and respect between Thailand and Cambodia
nodes.claim_html: The October 26 declaration commits both governments to stop spreading false information and to resolve differences peacefully. Less pressure to keep talking and reduce hostility toward the other national group works against understanding people who are different and accepting disagreement.

nodes.title: Personal Security: medical care and treatment
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted protects health when care is needed: less cost and supply risk for hospital devices used in surgery and infection control, less pressure on patients’ charges, less pressure to cut hospital and ambulance staff or reliable equipment, protection for some research on better tests and treatments, or more money left for medicine. Any one of them serves avoiding disease and protecting health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: everyday health
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted protects everyday health: cheaper nutritious food, less financial stress, less job insecurity, or less cost pressure on drinking-water treatment. Any one of them serves avoiding disease.

nodes.title: Personal Security: protection against fire, break-ins and injury
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted lowers a barrier to protection: alarms and fire alerts at home, helmets while cycling, or safety gear at work. Any one of them serves staying personally safe.

nodes.title: Personal Security: backup medical supplies in emergencies
nodes.claim_html: Weaker U.S. backup production of medical gloves puts at risk protection from infection and safe medical care when overseas supplies are disrupted, which gives a personal health reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Societal Security: defense supply and partners
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted supports the country’s defense: lower costs for military suppliers and what the military buys, less friction with defense partners, or cheaper backup supply options outside China. Any one of them supports a state able to defend its citizens.

nodes.title: Societal Security: essential water and hospital services
nodes.claim_html: Whichever you accepted, less cost pressure on water systems, or less cost and supply risk for hospital devices, helps keep services running that protect the public from disease and support emergency response. That strengthens the country’s ability to protect its citizens.

nodes.title: Societal Security: economic and financial stability
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted supports a stable country: less cost pressure on households, easier planning of investment in production capacity, or fewer tariff shocks to U.S. financial markets. Any one of them strengthens the economic base of a strong, stable state.

nodes.title: Societal Security: a legal check on emergency rule
nodes.claim_html: Enacting the resolution applies Congress’s legal check to this emergency. Keeping the President’s emergency power under standing rules protects dependable self-government and a secure, stable state.

nodes.title: Societal Security: weaker defense supply and security cooperation
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted weakens the country’s protection against threats: a smaller incentive to make military batteries in the United States, or less leverage for Malaysian and Cambodian promises on sensitive technology, defense minerals, sanctions on armed groups’ money and computer security. Any one of them gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tradition: worship music, Christmas customs and giving
nodes.claim_html: Each of these consequences you accepted lowers a cost of keeping a religious custom: familiar worship music, family Christmas customs, regular church offerings, or Christmas gift boxes that carry the gospel. Any one of them helps preserve established religious practice.

nodes.title: Tradition: tools for passing faith to children
nodes.claim_html: Southern Baptist teaching gives parents the duty to teach their children spiritual and moral values. Cheaper teaching aids help parents carry out that duty, which serves preserving Christian beliefs across generations.

nodes.title: Tradition: marriage and the provider role
nodes.claim_html: The Southern Baptist faith statement teaches lifelong marriage and a husband’s duty to provide for his family. Putting those religious roles at greater risk works against keeping them, which gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tradition: local congregations and their customs
nodes.claim_html: Local congregations are where families keep inherited worship customs alive across generations. Weakening them gives a reason to oppose the bill.
